title: Your values
hookLine: what matters most to you, in five words? the prophet Micah's courtroom answers in three (Micah 6:1-8)
tomorrow: why would the rabbis say: do good, even for the wrong reason?

lines: O MY PEOPLE, WHAT HAVE I DONE?
cards: The courtroom is outdoors. In the book of the prophet Micah, God calls his people to trial, and the mountains and hills are the jury. Then God speaks, and it isn't an accusation.
It sounds hurt: "O my people, what have I done unto thee?" The people scramble for an answer. What should we bring?
Burnt offerings? Calves? Thousands of rams?
Ten thousand rivers of oil? Our firstborn children? Every offer gets bigger and more desperate.

teach.h: DO JUSTLY, LOVE MERCY, WALK HUMBLY.
teach.b: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Three things, and none of them is an offering.
The whole bidding war of rams and oil was answering a question nobody asked.

teach.h: CHESED: KINDNESS THAT KEEPS SHOWING UP.
teach.b: The word translated mercy is the Hebrew chesed: loyal, steady kindness, the love that keeps showing up. Here's the teaching, held by Jews and Christians who read Micah as scripture.

teach.h: NOT A BIGGER GIFT: A WAY OF LIVING.
teach.b: In the Hebrew prophets, what God wants isn't a bigger gift. It's a way of living: fair dealing with others, kindness that doesn't quit, and humility before God. Micah fits the whole ask into one breath.
That's the challenge in today's line. What matters most to you, in five words? Not what would look good on a list.
Notice what the people in the story did. They went for the expensive answer, the one that cost the most and showed the most. The verdict was quieter and harder.

teach.h: VALUES YOU'D SEE ON A TUESDAY.
teach.b: Justice, mercy and humility are things you do on a Tuesday with the people in front of you.
So the test of a value isn't how grand it sounds. It's whether you'd recognize it in an ordinary afternoon. Micah's three are verbs: do, love, walk.

how: Jews read Micah among the prophets, and Christians read it in the Old Testament; there, 6:8 stands as the prophet's own summary of what the LORD requires.

o: a list of goals to reach in the next five years
what matters most to you, few enough to say in one breath
the rules your family or school gave you to follow

p: loyal kindness that keeps showing up
do justly, love mercy, walk humbly

s: in Micah 6, God asks for bigger offerings to settle the case
the people offer more and more; the verdict asks for justice, mercy and humility instead.
the word translated mercy in Micah 6:8 is the Hebrew chesed
loyal, steady kindness: the love that keeps showing up.
a good value should sound impressive on paper
Micah's three are verbs you can do on an ordinary afternoon.

games.q: your company asks everyone to pick 'core values' for a poster. the shortlist: excellence, innovation, impact. a coworker asks what Micah would have put up. what fits?
o: things done with people every day: fair dealing, steady kindness, humility.
the most impressive words, since values should impress whoever reads them.
nothing at all, since values only matter in religious settings.
games.why: the people in Micah reached for the expensive answer; the verdict was do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with God.

practice: Say five words that matter most to you out loud, one per breath, slowly. Then say them again, and with each one, call up a recent ordinary moment where you saw it, or missed it.

wordCard.voice: Your values: what matters most, small enough to say in one breath, like Micah's do justly, love mercy, walk humbly.

orig.note: Hebrew: loyal, steady kindness; the word the KJV renders 'mercy' in Micah 6:8.

carryVoice: Take this one: five words. Micah needed three, and every one was a verb. That's day 1590.
